claims.text: Systematic compositional variation can modify atomic-scale disorder in a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Atomic-scale disorder alters the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modulate electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength governs the superconducting transition temperature.
The starting material is a near-equiatomic, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
Substituting elements having different electronic properties will alter the degree of atomic-scale disorder.
Modified compositions will continue to satisfy the stated high-entropy-alloy compositional criterion.
Applying identical thermal and mechanical processing permits a controlled comparison among the compositions.
Measurements below 10 K will reliably determine the superconducting properties of the proposed alloys.
Increased chemical disorder modifies the density of states at the Fermi level.
Disorder-induced changes in the density of states alter the electron-phonon coupling involved in Cooper-pair formation.
An optimal level of atomic-scale disorder enhances the superconducting transition temperature by improving electron-phonon interactions.
Too little or excessive atomic-scale disorder will not produce the same superconducting enhancement as the optimum.
A composition having an optimized increase in atomic-scale disorder will exhibit a higher superconducting transition temperature than the baseline composition.
Changes in the density of states will correlate systematically with changes in superconducting transition temperature.
The original near-equiatomic alloy provides the baseline for transition temperature and transition behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions satisfying the minimum element-concentration requirement.
Phase separation or chemical ordering could independently affect superconductivity.
Powder X-ray diffraction can establish that each tested sample is single phase.
A lack of systematic correlation between disorder or density of states and transition temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows a nonmonotonic response with an unknown optimum and states that excessive or insufficient disorder may yield no enhancement, but the falsification rule treats any failure to obtain an enhancement as falsifying. A tested composition series could simply fail to span the unspecified optimum, so this branch of the rule does not logically contradict the mechanism.
